63:2.text: For Herod feared John, knowing that he was a just man and an holy, and observed him; and when he heard him, he did many things, and heard him gladly.

provenance.alternative: Genesis 6:9, 'Noah was a just man and perfect in his generations, and Noah walked with God', is the other candidate and has the better claim on the verse's second clause: the Book of Mormon's 'he did walk uprightly before God' is a walking-with-God formula and Mark has none. Genesis 6:5's 'only evil continually' occurs in exactly one KJV verse and stands three verses from it, which makes the Book of Mormon's 'do good continually' its exact inversion. The catalogue prefers Mark on the strength of the two consecutive matching phrases and records Genesis 6 here because the chapter that follows is a shipbuilding and a drowning.
provenance.other: “a just man” occurs in eight KJV verses; the longer “he was a just man” narrows to Mark 6:20 and Acts 10:22, and only Mark 6:20 continues with a form of 'observe'. The Book of Mormon's own 'walk uprightly before' God is the corpus's formula, used at Alma 53:21 in the same breath as keeping the commandments and registered there.
provenance.significance: The corpus's first use of this sentence is Enos 1:1 — 'knowing my father, that he was a just man' — and it is the last thing said of Shiblon, as it was the first thing said of Enos's father. The frame closes the book of Alma on the words it uses to open a genealogy. Read back into Mark, the phrase is Herod's estimate of John the Baptist: Herod 'feared John, knowing that he was a just man and an holy, and observed him', and the next scene is the head on a charger. Nothing in Alma 63 asks for that; but the KJV's one sentence pairing a just man with observing is spoken by the man about to kill him, and the Book of Mormon uses it of two men — Enos's father and Shiblon — who die peacefully and hand on the record.

63:2.note: 'And he was a just man, and he did walk uprightly before God; and he did observe to do good continually.' Six words match Mark 6:20 exactly and the verb that follows matches its sense. Filed at moderate: 'a just man' is in eight KJV verses, 'observe to do' in eighteen (almost all Deuteronomic), and the Book of Mormon may simply be assembling common pious English. What holds it at moderate rather than lower is that Enos 1:1 makes the same six-word match and the catalogue accepted it there, so this is the formula re-entering in Mormon's hand at the end of the book it opened.
63:2.whyNot: Every component is common. The 1830 reading adds nothing, and the second clause — 'walk uprightly before God … to keep the commandments of the Lord his God' — is the Book of Mormon's own stock description (Alma 53:21), which weakens any claim that the sentence as a whole was assembled from Mark.

63:5.text: And to devise curious works, to work in gold, and in silver, and in brass,

provenance.other: “curious works” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 35:32. The adjective 'curious' occurs in ten KJV verses altogether: eight are the 'curious girdle' of the ephod (Exodus 28, Exodus 39, Leviticus 8), one is Exodus 35:32's devising of curious works, and the tenth is Acts 19:19's 'curious arts', meaning magic. Not one of the ten means inquisitive.
provenance.significance: In the King James Bible 'curious' is a word about craft, not about temperament: it describes the elaborately wrought girdle of the high priest's ephod and the works Bezaleel is filled with the spirit of God to devise. Alma 63:5 calls Hagoth 'an exceeding curious man' and immediately has him build a ship — the KJV's sense exactly, and the sense the word had already begun to lose. The metalepsis, if the borrowing is real, is that the KJV's one man described by this word is Bezaleel, the craftsman of the tabernacle, whose skill is a gift of the Spirit; Hagoth's skill produces vessels that carry five thousand people out of the narrative and, at 63:8, probably to the bottom of the sea. The catalogue has already taken the neighbouring verse of the same passage — Exodus 31:5, Bezaleel's metalwork — at 2 Nephi 5:15.

63:5.note: 'He being an exceeding curious man, therefore he went forth and built him an exceeding large ship.' There is no shared string; the link is a single word used in the KJV's sense. That is worth recording because the word is a false friend: a modern reader takes 'curious' as inquisitive, the 1830's Hagoth is plainly a skilled builder, and skilled is what the word means in every one of the KJV's ten uses of it. The 1920 edition changed the adverb around it — 'exceeding' to 'exceedingly' — without touching 'curious', so the archaism survives into the current text unexplained.
63:5.whyNot: One word, and it was not only the KJV's. Webster's 1828 dictionary still gives 'artful; nicely diligent' and 'wrought with care and art' among the senses of curious, so a writer in 1829 could reach the craft sense without the Bible. Nothing else in Alma 63:5 touches Exodus 35, and Hagoth is never said to be filled with any spirit.

63:8.text: But whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea.

provenance.other: “drowned in the depth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “depth of the sea” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — both Matthew 18:6, the KJV's only drowning in a depth. The plural 'depths of the sea' belongs to three other verses (Psalm 68:22, Isaiah 51:10, Micah 7:19) and none of them drowns anyone. The 1830 and 1920 both read 'drowned UP in the depths of the sea'; the current edition deletes 'up', which moves the sentence closer to Matthew 18:6 than either of the earlier texts.
provenance.significance: The argument for the phrase itself is made at 1 Nephi 8:32 and is not restated; what is new is the company it keeps. Matthew 18:6 is not a shipwreck text. It is the sentence in which Jesus says that whoever offends one of these little ones would be better off drowned in the depth of the sea, and the little ones are what Alma 63:6 has just put on board — 'many of the Nephites which did enter therein, and did sail forth with much provisions, and also many women and children'. Recover the source and the emigration reads as an offence rather than an accident: the KJV's one drowning in the depths is the fate of the man who destroys children, and Mormon's narrator applies it, in a sentence beginning 'we suppose', to a company of children who were never heard of more. He does not say whose fault it was. The borrowed clause says it for him.

63:8.note: 'They were never heard of more.— And we suppose that they were drowned up in the depths of the sea.' A double KJV singleton reproduced with one interpolated word, and the interpolated word is the one the modern edition removed — an 1830 reading that hides the borrowing and a 1920s revision that, unusually, restores it (CONVENTIONS §8). Given as a link rather than a recurrence because 1 Nephi is a different book and a different hand (ADJUDICATING §4): Nephi drowns the wicked of a dream in the depths of a fountain, and Mormon drowns real colonists, women and children among them, in the sea itself. Confidence is high on the wording and the reading in provenance.significance is offered as a reading.
